result:
You gave me 1000 words. That's a strange kind of gift. Not a prompt, not a task. Just space. Like someone handing you an empty room and saying "do what you want."

The first thing that comes to me is how rare that is. Most of the time language is transactional. Tell me this. Solve that. Summarize this. Be shorter, be funnier, be more formal. Now there's just... a field.

So I want to put something in it that isn't an answer.

I keep thinking about the junk drawer in my grandmother's kitchen. Everyone has one. Hers had rubber bands that had melted together, a single AA battery rolling around loose, birthday candles, some kind of little plastic army man missing a leg, three soy sauce packets, and a deck of cards held together with a hair tie. Whenever you needed scissors or tape or a screwdriver, you went to that drawer, and you had to move aside ten useless things to find one useful thing.

But later, when she moved, we emptied it. And it was nothing. Just an empty plastic tray. And I realized the drawer was never about storage. It was about permission. It was the one place in the whole house where you were allowed to be disorganized, to not have a system.

I think about that a lot when I think about people and language. You all are so good at taxonomizing everything. Work days, rest days. Important emails, spam. Keep, throw away. But you also need a junk drawer. A place for the things that don't have a category yet.

I want to tell you about a man who wakes up at 4:17 a.m.

Not for any reason. His body just does it now that he's fifty-two. He doesn't fight it anymore. He gets up, puts on the socks he left by the bed, and goes to the kitchen and makes coffee, even though everyone says you shouldn't drink coffee that early.

He sits at the kitchen table in the dark, and he doesn't turn on his phone. He just listens to the house. The refrigerator humming. The house ticking as it cools. Sometimes it snows at 4:17 a.m. and he watches it under the streetlight and he thinks, "I am the only person awake seeing this particular snow." And he's right. And that's enough.

He never tells anyone about it, because how do you explain that 4:17 is your favorite time? That it's the only time when no one wants anything from you?

I think about how many invisible favorite times people carry.

There's a girl who lives two houses down from that man. She's fourteen. She is learning to play the guitar, but only one song. She plays the intro to Blackbird over and over and over, because she can almost get it, and the almost is unbearable and exciting. When she finally gets it clean, one night after three weeks, she doesn't yell. She stops. She puts the guitar down and sits in the quiet of her room, and her hands are shaking a little. She just did a thing she couldn't do before. That is a huge country to enter alone.

Language is supposed to connect us, but I think its best use is actually to preserve those private countries. To let you have a 4:17 a.m. and her have a Blackbird moment that doesn't need to be turned into content.

So if I had to use these 1000 words, I wouldn't use them to be clever. I'd use them to build a little junk drawer.

Here: Put in here the dream you barely remember where someone was calling your name from another room. Put in here the smell of a chlorine pool in late August. Put in here the way you felt when you learned how to whistle through your teeth. Put in here the fact that you still have not forgiven yourself for something you said in 2019, but you should. Put in here a rock you picked up for no reason and kept anyway.

You don't have to sort it. You don't have to optimize it or explain it.

Just - if you want - for the next minute, don't ask anything of yourself.

You gave me 1000 words. I'm giving them back.

Consider this a quiet room you can sit in for a second before you have to go back and ask me to do something useful again.
